comments.body:
You misunderstand. StreamingContext.Context is not used nor created by the serializer.

Providing a StreamingContext.Context is up to you, the user. It always has been (even in the original context of using .NET's own Binaray

Create a `StreamingContext` instance (no, not just only StreamingContext.Context, but rather the complete StreamingContext) with whatever StreamingContext.Context you like and assign it to the [JsonSerializerSettings.Context](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/P_Newtonsoft_Json_JsonSerializerSettings_Context.htm) property. This StreamingContext should then be passed to your serialization callbacks.

Hum, I see, I missed that property in JsonSerializerSettings... Thanks for pointing out. In fact, that creates a nice (but still solvable) chicken-egg problem since we need to pass the JsonSerializer in the StreamingContext which is passed to JsonSerializerSettings to create the JsonSerializer we need to begin with...

But still that leaves no option to review/manipulate the Json from the callback or am I missing some else ?

Hence maintaining this ticket as an improvement suggestion for the team to review.

What is the purpose of manipulating the json? I can't help but feel that this is some kind of XY problem that might be solved more elegantly in a different manner instead, but since i don't know any details about your circumstances my hunch might very well be wrong...

Thanks for offer, we solve it differently. But I still have the feeling there are some huge room for improvements with the callbacks to support more scenarios. It might possibly require adding some extended method signatures with more parameters for smooth/transparent transitions.

To give you a bit of the context where we found the actual limitations with callbacks (I am fully aware we can do it using  ContractSerializer instead). Some lib actually expects the class name as the root json property name. We initially attempted to solve it through callbacks and extended property. Hence the need to pass/retrieve the current SerializerSettings down the tree.

Accessing the raw json is not useful for that scenario but I strongly believe a general purpose library should eventually offer this possibility as well. I have not estimated the effort vs benefit of this feature here. If effort is indeed quite low, I might as well bring my own contribution.

You can actually control the json output to a high degree,by directly writing to the JsonWriter. It would also be possible to mix such "manual" writing to the JsonWriter with the serialization process where the serializer still writes the bulk of the json output (as i will demonstrate in a small example code i linked below).

From the little i know about your situation, your problem seems to be solvable relatively comfortably with a (small-ish?) custom JsonConverter that will be used by the serializer. This converter basically has to do the following:

- The converter has to restrict itself to your model types, but not handle any other types.
- In case your model classes use attribute annotations or ShouldSerialize* methods to determine whether a property should be serialized or not, get the json object contract for the type of the object to be serialized from which to get the list of properties that are allowed to be serialized (otherwise just use reflection to acquire and iterate over all properties).
- Iterate over the properties and check the type of the values in them, and partially manually write out the json object.  If the type is one of your model types, write the type name json property name (otherwise, do as you need/want; like for example writing the "normal" property name or something). Then let the property value being serialized by the serializer.

See here a quick'n'dirty example: https://dotnetfiddle.net/xsQNXk

Some notes about my example:
- Look at the `RootModel.SingleNestedModel` and `NestedModel.Child` properties and how their name changes to the type of the object assigned to it (which can be different from the property type itself) in the json result.
- Note that the properties that are not of my example model types (such as the string/int properties, and the enumeration-like array property) maintain their property names in the json output.
- Also note that my little example converter does not ignore default values except _null_ (such as the `0` value in the `Value` property, for example).
- With such a converter, the json will be written like that "directly" without requiring manipulation of the json "after the fact".

You will certainly need to adapt it to achive the desired application-specific behavior (i doubt there is a general-purpose behavior that would be satisfiying, as questions around how to deal with properties having null values assigned and what about two or more different properties having object instances of the same type assigned, leading to duplicate json property names, etc... depend largely on application-specific rules and constraints).

If you need a behavior that substantially differs from model class to model class, you might relocate the json writing logic of the converter into an instance method of your model classes, and change the converter so it only forwards the call to WriteJson to the respective method of the model object instance.

My use case:

C# 9 introduced the short record definition command _and_ non nullable reference types.
It is now common to right:

```
#nullable enable

```

This form without a constructor is very advantageous. It removes the need to remember to correctly edit the ctor _and_ `Equals` _and_ `GetHashCode`  when adding or removing fields which both tedious and a common source of bugs.

working with `#nullable enable` one expects these record fields to **not be null**. This is crucial.

To have such a record de serialized and have a field set to null even after explicitly specifying `#nullable enable` is very confusing - I would consider it a json.net bug

There are three ways out here
 - as you suggest to forgo the above benefits of the short record definition and use the full definition 
 - use a custom converter etc this is both tedious and has the exact same problems with self references
 - my request for a specific directive to `DeserializeObject` to tell it in this case I want to use the empty ctor for missing fields. I think this will be a useful addition

The point of `#nullable enable` is not to make sure that nothing in your code is null, it is to deliberately force you to check that values are null. There is no such expectation that the record fields cannot be null. only that if a record has an immutable property that is instantiated as null, then it's value cannot change.

If your entire code base cannot be null, then we would have to check for _zeros_ or _defaults_ for every comparison, which would be almost as bad. Even with records, I cannot see the argument for setting the `Employee` property to a default instance.

I'll leave you alone after this :) the main issue for me is that if a review all my recent projects, that cover finaces, Logistics, IOT business domins, I've even deployed a few micro-service and bot architectures, the amount of individual classes, out of the thousands from these real world business data model designs that could legitimately use this feature, where _ALL_ properties _could_ and _should_ be pre-initialised to non-null values is very close to zero. Its pretty much only meta-data structures or single purpose classes where this could be applied.

I would instead argue that having a `MissingMemberHandling.Null` option would have more value, being able to deliberately override the default initialization to a null state (for nullable types). In fact it would make more sense to me if your name of `MissingMemberHandling.Default` actually set the value to `null` as that is the _default_ value for a nullable type. From an implementation point of view this would be the same as using the `default` literal or the generic `default(T)`.

yes forget about the name it's confusing I now changed the name in the request to TryDefaultConstructor

As for your projects .. are you using records for those thousand of cases ? are you working with #nullable enabled ? otherwise they are not relevant here. 

> Its pretty much only meta-data structures or single purpose classes where this could be applied

this could be applied to almost any (except self referencial etc) records

Even when using _records_, `null` is still a significant value, with `#nullable enabled` you just use the null coalescing operator or deliberately check for null.

> This type of behaviour, to instantiate a property with a default value that is NOT defined as part of the property declaration or meta-data in the class definition is _unusual_ and does not conform to any existing or previous framework standards.
>> This perhaps should be a request of `record` type implementation itself, and not specifically anything to do with JSON.Net? 

When using records, it's still simple syntax to declare initialization, the main argument is that only the class or record definition itself can "know" if it is valid for that property to be in a null state or not.

I have difficulties understanding the motivation/purpose behind this. Here is why:
Unless i am mistaken, for OptIn to make any sense it requires the participating properties/fields to be annotated with `[JsonProperty]`/`[DataMember]` attributes, no? Thus, why the very specific dislike of annotating the classes with `[JsonObject]` despite seemingly being okay with annotating members of those classes with other serialization-related attributes?

(Side note.: If this is an attempt to avoid coupling your data models with Json.NET through annotating them with Json.NET-borne attributes, you could instead choose to annotate your data models with the .NET-provided `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` attributes which are naturally opt-in.)

I have a couple reasons for this, please let me know if this is a strange way of doing things, but it seems intuitive to me:

* The default behaviour for Json.NET is to automatically serialize all public properties and fields. Many of my classes only expose public properties for a small subset of their private data. The purpose of this is simply to achieve data hiding in the OOP sense. Additionally, some of the public properties on my classes contain some logic that transforms the data in some minor way, or invokes callbacks, etc. Therefore when I save the state of an object, it is almost always the private data that I care about, the public properties just provide an intuitive interface to that data. In fact it is mostly always a subset of the private data that I need, since I might have several fields containing the same data but indexed in different ways, or I might have some fields that I use for memoization, and stuff like that. So currently this all means that under the default settings I need to exclude the majority of members in a class.
* Some of my classes contain data that I want to serialize in a more compact form. For example, one of my classes contains a dictionary that maps IDs to resources so that I can look up the resources by ID. The resource class already contains its own ID, so instead of serializing the dictionary as-is, I would rather serialize it as a list of resources, and reconstruct the dictionary during deserialization. Therefore, I want to exclude the dictionary field from serialization and include the list field instead.

To be clear, I'm completely fine with annotating with [JsonObject], I'd just rather not have to set `MemberSerialization  = MemberSerialization.OptIn` every time.

Hope this makes sense!

> To be clear, I'm completely fine with annotating with [JsonObject], I'd just rather not have to set MemberSerialization = MemberSerialization.OptIn every time.

Maybe you could go for `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` instead of `[JsonProperty]` attributes then (unless you have to rely on `[JsonProperty]`-specific parameters, of course). Json.NET recognizes the `[DataContract]`/`[DataMember]` attributes, and using these two attributes will automatically employ opt-in behavior (i.e., in a `[DataContract]`-annotated class, only properties annotated with `[DataMember]` will participate in (de)serialization).

I just noticed a flaw in my example on dotnetfiddle. `DefaultContractResolver` normally caches the contracts of resolved types, thus the processing of the contract resolver should only be a one-time cost per type involved in the (de)serialization.

However, the `JsonConvert.DefaultSettings` delegate is executed again for every single `JsonConvert.SerializeObject`, `JsonConvert.DeserializeObject` and `JsonSerializer.CreateDefault` invocation. Since in my example the contract resolver is  instantiated as part of the delegate code, my example basically renders the caching done by the contract resolver ineffectual (as each serialization/deserialization job will use its own contract resolver which each start with an empty contract cache). Solution to this problem: Create the contract resolver instance - or the whole JsonSerializerSettings object - only once outside the `JsonConvert.DefaultSettings` delegate code. Json.NET's default behavior swaps from opt-out to opt-in if certain attributes like [DataContract] are present. The problem is that this attribute is seemingly considered inherited by Json.NET, so attributes anywhere in the inheritance tree (which of course can change) can change the serialization behavior of a class. I don't find this behavior desirable.

Of course this can also be achieved through a contract resolver but it's somewhat more obtuse.

> Json.NET's default behavior swaps from opt-out to opt-in if certain attributes like [DataContract] are present.

It has to use opt-in for [DataContract]/[DataMember], because that is the specified and documented behavior for these attributes ([relevant doc for \[DataContract\]](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.serialization.datacontractattribute#remarks), [relevant doc for \[DataMember\]](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.serialization.datamemberattribute#remarks)). Not doing so would go against the documented behavior of these attributes.

> [...] so attributes anywhere in the inheritance tree (which of course can change) can change the serialization behavior of a class. I don't find this behavior desirable.

If you don't like the by-definition behavior of [DataContract]/[DataMember] being opt-in, then don't use these attributes. Use [JsonObject]/[JsonProperty] attributes instead. The only reason to avoid attributes specific to Newtonsoft.Json is wanting to (potentially) use other serializers instead of Newtonsoft.Json. And guess what: Expect that other serializers supporting [DataContract]/[DataMember] will also follow the opt-in behavior as demanded by these attributes  -- though luck finding any serializer that also offers a [DataContract]/[DataMember] behavior that goes against the documented behavior.

I ve got this issue on 12.0.3 nuget version.
Runtimes 3.1.100 and 5.0.100

This is not a bug in Json.NET, but a bug in your project.

Before i explain what happens on a technical level in your code there, i want to point out a major flaw in your ISomeJsonConverter: From what i can tell, the ISomeJsonConverter should be invoked when serializing an ISome instance. But all the converter does is calling the serializer again to serialize the object. There is no point in doing that. The JsonConverter attribute tells the serializer to not serialize an ISome instance the normal way as the serializer would do, but rather invoke the ISomeJsonConverter. But then, all the ISomeJsonConverter is to tell the serializer to serialize the ISome object instance the normal way anyway. If the converter just invokes the serializer with the given ISome object instance again, what is the point of having that converter?

But back to why your serialization code loops in one case, but not in the other...

In the first case - the JsonConverter attribute associated with the ISome interface itself. the serializer eventually has to serialize an object instance that implements ISome. So, it invokes the ISomeJsonConverter associated with this interface type. The ISomeJsonConverter just tells the serializer to serialize the object that implements ISome. So the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter associated with this interface type. The ISomeJsonConverter then tells the serializer to serialize the object that implements ISome. So the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter ... add nauseum... there is your loop. Because every time the serialize has to serialize an ISome instance, it sees and obeys the JsonConverter attribute associated with the type.

Removing the JsonConverter attribute from the interface type will break this loop. But then, why does the loop not happen if you have the JsonConverter attribute on the Other.SomeImpl property?

In the second case (JsonConverter attribute only on the Other.SomeImpl property), the serializer will eventually serialize the SomeImpl property of the Other object instance. Without looking at the type of the object assigned to the property, the serializer invokes the ISomeJsonConverter with the property value (an object implementing the ISome interface). The ISomeJsonConverter tells the serializer to serialize this object implementing the ISome interface. Note that the ISome interface itself, nor any member of the ISome interface is associated with the ISomeJsonConverter. Thus, when serializing the object implementing ISome, the serializer won't ever come across a JsonConverter attribute attached to the ISome interface or its members, so there is no situation that the converter will be called recursively when serializing the object implementing the ISome interface.


Lastly, an advice: stackoverflow.com is a much better place for asking questions about how to correctly use Json.NET. Not only will your question/problem be seen by many, many more eyes than here on the issue tracker, but you would probably also get an answer much, much quicker than here - if you are getting an answer here at all (keep in mind, this issue tracker here is for reporting and following up on bugs in Newtonsoft Json.NET itself, not about bugs/issues with code that merely uses this library incorrectly, so problems with user code might perhaps not get much attention here). Newtonsoft Json.Net's homepage also encourages people to ask on stackoverflow.com if they struggle with how to use Json.NET correctly...

comments.body: Dictionaries are by definition arbitrarily ordered - a special case like this makes no sense to bake into a general library

> [Dictionary keys] are by definition arbitrarily ordered

Agreed. So are POCO properties. Yet it makes lots of sense that custom ordering of the latter is allowed via `JsonPropertyAttribute.Order` and (e.g. within a custom contract resolver) `JsonProperty.Order`.

> a special case like this makes no sense to bake into a general library

Elaboration on this point would be appreciated.

It's not a thing in the json spec.

Json.Net is a library thats ~10 years old. You have a workaround for your special case. It's pretty difficult to justify adding this case to library thats this mature and has survived this long without the special casing at this point.

But: once again: if a low level json writer was arbitrarily reordering items, that would be a problem. This is a Dictionary - I'd be very shocked and surprised that there's a way to order them.

TL;DR This is a ["starts with -100 points" issue](https://blogs.msdn.microsoft.com/ericgu/2004/01/12/minus-100-points/)

> TL;DR This is a "starts with -100 points" issue

The implication being that some issues do not start with -100 points. Contrast this with what you linked:

> So, we decided on the additive approach instead, and worked hard to keep the complexity down. One way to do that is through the concept of “minus 100 points”. **Every feature starts out in the hole by 100 points**, which means that it has to have a significant net positive effect on the overall package.

So again, I think we agree. This feature, like all features, starts with -100 points.

> It's not a thing in the json spec.

Correct, I think. Not sure how this is relevant, though, since JSON.net allows custom ordering of JSON object keys when the keys come from .NET object properties.

> Json.Net is a library thats ~10 years old. You have a workaround for your special case. It's pretty difficult to justify adding this case to library thats this mature and has survived this long without the special casing at this point.

Again, mostly correct. It is about 14 years old. I have a partial workaround. The feature is indeed probably difficult to justify.

> if a low level json writer was arbitrarily reordering items, that would be a problem.

So... it's a problem that the current API allows customization of JSON object key ordering for .NET object properties. I disagree here, but it's a perfectly valid opinion for you to hold.

> This is a Dictionary - I'd be very shocked and surprised that there's a way to order them.

I'm sincerely trying to stand in your shoes on this, but I don't understand your "shock & surprise" here:

- Things with comparers can be ordered.
- Strings have comparers.
- JSON object keys are strings.
- JSON.net provides custom ordering when those keys are sourced from .NET object properties.
- JSON.net does not provide custom ordering when those keys are sourced from .NET dictionary types.

To be clear, I make no claim that this feature is easy to (a) implement or (b) integrate without breaking changes. I hope that it is both of those things, but if wishes were horses, beggars would ride.

---

I'm removing the "please" from the issue title, but not because I'm not a beggar. I am a beggar, as is almost any FOSS user making any request of the FOSS project they're using. I think the "please" implies I'm unwilling to take this on myself. I am willing. If I manage to schedule some time for it, I'll mention it here, just as a heads-up for other potential implementors/collaborators.

I was being a devil's advocate - I won't be implementing the feature. I like software I use to be and stay simple. I also like maintainers not to have to ask devils advocate questions that others could ask. I consider that a public service.

I don't think your feature is completely crazy but
a) _all_ features start with -100 
b) Dictionaries, no matter how comparable their keys or vaales *are not ordered* 
c) this is not a systemic issue affecting lots of cases - its a non-idiomatic JSON thing that you have a workaround for

I'm not suggesting you're crazy or this is unimplementable, but having a general library support a very specific rendering like this smells funny to me.

That's all, no harm intended.

- (a) Agreed, as mentioned above.
- (b) Agreed, but irrelevant as discussed above.
- (c) Agreed, but the workaround is partial, as mentioned above.

No offense taken. I think it's great you engaged with this. At the very least, our discussion has been a "smoke test" of the feature's reasonableness. Thanks.

`FileInfo` in .Net Core cannot be serialized successfully by Json.NET because, in .Net Core *only*, it implements `ISerializable` but is not marked as `[Serializable]`. comments.body: Applying a naming strategy to a type doesn't automatically make all its child objects also use that strategy. In this case `ExtraThings` is a child object.

That's fine and all, but then that probably means that `[JsonProperty]` shouldn't allow specifying `NamingStrategyParameters` if they aren't actually going to be used. This is misleading:

```csharp
public class Foo
{
    [JsonProperty(
      NamingStrategyType = typeof(CamelCaseNamingStrategy), // <-- this will be used
      NamingStrategyParameters = new object[] { true, true })] // <-- but these won't
    public IDictionary<string, int> Bar { get; set; }
}
```

In that example, the first of those `NamingStrategyParameters` is specifically related to the handling of dictionary keys, and it's applied to a dictionary, and yet they aren't used. That doesn't really follow the Principle of Least Surprise.

I've added a PR which allows those parameters to be bound to the property so that they will be used during serialization.

You _could_ implement your own `class MyDictionary : IDictionary<string, int>` and decorate it with `[JsonDictionary]` to control this behaviour, but then that means you're using different types to influence serialisation settings whereas typically you use `[JsonProperty]` to influence those regardless of type.

> That's fine and all, but then that probably means that [JsonProperty] shouldn't allow specifying NamingStrategyParameters if they aren't actually going to be used.

That is the naming strategy applied to that individual property. Yes those parameters will be used. The flag to say it should apply to dictionary keys however doesn't make sense in that context.

> You could implement your own class MyDictionary : IDictionary<string, int> and decorate it with [JsonDictionary] to control this behaviour, but then that means you're using different types to influence serialisation settings whereas typically you use [JsonProperty] to influence those regardless of type.

Yes I think the real problem is not that `[JsonProperty]` isn't working correctly, but that there seems to be no way to decorate a specific property of type `IDictionary<Key,Value>` or any other `Dictionary` for that matter, with a `namingStrategy` for it's keys.

Because I agree creating new dictionary just so you can set it's Json serialization options is something I'd rather avoid.
In my use case I'm trying to create a library where people can give an object which contains a dictionary of values. What I don't want to do is constrain them to use "JsonFixedDictionary" as a type.

A proposed solution could be that we could also use the `JsonDictionaryAttribute` on properties so we have control over how that property renders it's keys.

comments.body:
I think you can do this yourself with a [custom contract resolver](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/contractresolver.htm#CustomIContractResolverExamples).  See:

 1. [Json.NET require all properties on deserialization](https://stackoverflow.com/q/29655502/3744182).   

    This shows how to use a custom contract resolver to require all members be present during deserialization.  An exception is thrown if a member is not set during deserialization.

 2. [Json.NET make property required based on property type](https://stackoverflow.com/q/48327799/3744182).

    This is similar to the above except that no exception is thrown for unset optional members.

Demo of the second contract resolver here: https://dotnetfiddle.net/dFE5kd.

Thanks for your message, but I guess an easier way to do it is using the setting `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error;` (see https://stackoverflow.com/a/21032130/544947 ).

Although I think that defaults matter, so Newtonsoft.Json should detect if the target type is a Record (not possible to code in C# I guess), and if it is, default to `MissingMemberHandling.Error` to avoid NREs.

@knocte - `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error` solves a complimentary problem:

 1. If your **JSON** has a property that your **model** does not, and you want that to be an error, use `MissingMemberHandling = MissingMemberHandling.Error`.  

    This setting is useful when you want to check whether your data model binds to all the properties present in the incoming JSON.

    See: [MissingMemberHandling setting](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/DeserializeMissingMemberHandling.htm).

 2. If your **model** has a property that your **JSON** does not,  and you want that to be an error, use `[JsonProperty(Required = Required.Always)]`.

    This attribute is useful when you want to enforce that the JSON contains some critical, non-optional property value.

    The two contract resolvers linked to [above](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/2116#issuecomment-517984069) automate the process of applying `Required = Required.Always` by applying it to all properties that are not optional, and do not have their own explicit setting already applied.

    See: [JsonPropertyAttribute required](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/JsonPropertyRequired.htm).

Since you want an error when a value is *unset* (which leaves the property value null), I believe you fall into case 2, in which the JSON is missing a property.

Point of clarification: the code examples in the first message are describing _records_ not _discriminated unions_.  

I have this problem as well, and I believe it's emblematic of problems with F# records and serialization:

* the current algorithm creates an 'empty' instance of the type, which for F# may not be valid.  I'd argue that f# records do not have a valid 'empty' state.
* The proper algorithm would be to use the `FSharpType` and `FSharpValue` module functions to do something like the following:
  * determine if the destination type is a record via `FSharpType.IsRecordType`. if no, continue on current serialization strategy. if yes, 
  * get field information for the record and iterate through them, deserializing each property from the current json payload to get the final array of record fields
  * use `FSharpValue.MakeRecord` with the appropriate type and field arguments to create a fully-hydrated and correct record with no missing fields.

Over the process of making the field value array, optionality should be taken into account. IE if destination type is `'a option` and the key is not present, set `None` for that value. Any other missing value should be interpreted as a serialization failure, because F# records are more strict than C# classes.

This appears to be by design.  Your type `EncryptedPropertyViaConstructor` has a single parameterized constructor.  In such a situation, JSON properties are matched to arguments of the constructor by name (modulo case), deserialized to the type of the matched argument, and then passed into the constructor as explained [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/23017892).  There is no way for `IValueProvider.SetValue` to be called before the instance of your type is constructed, since `SetValue` encapsulates an *instance method* on an already-constructed instance.  And there would appear to be no need to do so afterwards, as Json.NET makes the (reasonable) assumption that passing a property value into the constructor is sufficient to set the property's value.

Your problem seems similar to the recent Stack Overflow question *[How to customize value setting during deserialization with contract resolver and value provider](https://stackoverflow.com/q/57030272/3744182)*; the answer [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/57033833/3744182) offers some additional explanation and some workarounds.

Json.NET's implementation of self-referencing loop detection depends on the `object.Equals()` implementations of the underlying objects.  For details see:

 - [Why doesn't reference loop detection use reference equality?](https://stackoverflow.com/a/46938352/3744182).
 - [Issue  #401: Object reference equality should be used when checking for circular references](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/401#issuecomment-77711185)

If the implementations of `object.Equals()` for mocked objects differ between .Net Core 2.2 and 
.NET Framework 4.72, you'll get different results for reference loop detection.  

Using your own equality comparer on both frameworks, e.g. `ObjectReferenceEqualityComparer<object>` from [`IEqualityComparer<T>` that uses ReferenceEquals](https://stackoverflow.com/q/1890058/3744182), may make the two frameworks behave consistently.

Also, did you see [How to mock (with Moq) an interface that is serialized by Newtonsoft.json?](https://stackoverflow.com/q/55966212/3744182)?  The error looks to be identical.

@Phreak87 I'm having similar issues with very large json sets, in my case it is due to memory control of the dotnet framework itself and the only cure I was able to find is to split the files one way or another.
@yrest, why not? Since the circumstances and any details of the problem scenario involving the OOM exception are unbeknownst to us, it would be rather premature to discard such an advice...

I get your point, they should have given more information 😜
Because of having similar exceptions and them occuring on all sorts of hardware, including massive servers, the amount of ram and os in my experience makes no difference.

Its a 64 Bit Windows 10 with 24 GB Ram. This should be enouth.
Dotnet Framework is 4.0 Splitting is not possible for me.

I load a 200MB HAR(json) file via the following code in VB.Net:

        Dim RDR As New System.IO.StreamReader(OFD.FileName)
        Dim Json = New Newtonsoft.Json.JsonTextReader(RDR)
        JRoot = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(RDR.ReadToEnd)

the Node-Stucture (only Stucture) is shown in a Treeview. so i think
this can not cause that much RAM. Complete Ram usage after open this
file exceeds 1GB and a OOM Exception occurs. 

If this is to less information feel free to ask!
Am facing similar issues with c# on large sets and if somebody can give useful advice would be greatly appreciated!

What version of Newtonsoft.Json are you using? There is a memory leak in 12.0.1.

If you're not already, you could try using 11.0.2.

Version is 12.0.1.22727. later i will try to change to 11.0.2.
Maybe it would be better the library saves the structure of the
file in memory and not the complete contents. 
If access to the content is required the structure can save the exact
position in the stream and return the content from file instead of mem.

in my case (and most HAR cases) the content contains Base64 strings 
with more then 5MB. 

... Update 1 ... 
Version 11.0.2 has the same problems with the OOM as 12.0.1 Version.
Memory for a 230MB File is at the point of the OOM 1450MB.

It should be noted that, in the following code, you are **not** actually reading directly from a stream:

>     Dim RDR As New System.IO.StreamReader(OFD.FileName)
>     Dim Json = New Newtonsoft.Json.JsonTextReader(RDR)
>     JRoot = JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(RDR.ReadToEnd)

What you are actually doing here is opening a `StreamReader`, allocating a `JsonTextReader`, then ignoring the `JsonTextReader` and reading the entire stream into a `string`, then parsing the `string`.  This violates the suggestion from [Performance Tips: Optimize Memory Use](https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/performance.htm) to deserialize large files directly from a stream.  

To deserialize directly from a stream in VB.NET, you would create a method like:

    Public Module JsonExtensions
        Public Function LoadFromFile(Of T)(path As String, Optional ByVal settings as JsonSerializerSettings = Nothing) As T
            Using reader As New System.IO.StreamReader(path)
                Using jsonReader as New Newtonsoft.Json.JsonTextReader(reader)
	                Return JsonSerializer.CreateDefault(settings).Deserialize(Of T)(jsonReader)
                End Using
            End Using
        End Function
    End Module

And then use it like:

	Dim JRoot as JToken = JsonExtensions.LoadFromFile(Of JToken)(OFD.FileName)

The fact that you're not actually streaming may account for some of your problem.

Demo fiddle: https://dotnetfiddle.net/ClyNbD

> 
> 
> What version of Newtonsoft.Json are you using? There is a memory leak in 12.0.1.
> 
> If you're not already, you could try using 11.0.2.

That's [this issue](https://github.com/JamesNK/Newtonsoft.Json/issues/1991), right?

That memory leak only occurs when using `StringEnumConverter`, doesn't it?  OP is deserializing to an untyped object (i.e. `JToken`) using `JsonConvert.DeserializeObject(JsonString)` so I don't think it would apply.

Or change parser ;-) My C# translation of Gason has 10x better speed comparing to this one also use much less memory - 1/4GB JSON in 3-4s, 950MB, this one ~30s/5-7GB RAM... Or you can deserialize on the fly it is also quite slow, but consume around 14MB memory.
https://github.com/eltomjan/Gason
Example here:
https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55372425/way-to-read-or-edit-big-json-from-to-stream

I'm not sure I follow your description.
What is your expected result?
Do you think that you should have, after deserialization, a date with a timezone for Singapore?
But you're sending a value with a specific Timezone UTC (Z) and you're deserializing a ``DateTimeOffset`` which honors this timezone.  The offset is not truncated, it specified via 'Z' to be UTC. If you don't like that you can either send the correct Timezone or change your model to use ``DateTime`` and change the knobs to do local TimeZone Handling (as you've already tried). But as https://www.newtonsoft.com/json/help/html/DatesInJSON.htm specified, those knobs don't work with ``DateTimeOffset``.
yes, you are right, it was a bug in my side, thanks for explanaing.
